P0.p: General heading for tales and beliefs about royalty and the nobility, meaning kings, queens, princes and nobles.

P3.p: The child born from a marriage of a brother and sister of the highest chiefly rank is a god.

P10.p: General heading for kings as a category, covering tales and beliefs about rulers.

P10.1.p: A special place where royal children are born.

P11.p: General heading for how kings are chosen or selected to rule.

P11.0.1.p: A prophecy says that whichever brother first kisses a saint will become king.

P11.0.2.p: The trees choose a king of the forest, selecting one of their number to rule them.

P11.0.2.1.p: The bramble (blackberry bush) is chosen as king of the trees.

P11.1.r: *Egerton JAOS XXXIII 158; Krappe Revue Hispanique LVI (1922) 5—24; *Penzer V 175ff.; *Chauvin VI 75 No. 239; India: Thompson-Balys.
P11.1.p: Kings are chosen by the will of God or the gods.

P11.1.1.p: Kings are chosen by drawing lots.

P11.2.p: A kingship is awarded to whoever wins a contest held to choose the next king.

P11.2.1.p: Princes compete to find the greatest fault in their father, the king, and the one who can find none, the youngest, is chosen as king.

P11.2.2.p: A king is chosen through a contest, with the winner taking the throne.

P11.2.2.1.p: Of two giant brothers, the one who performs the greatest feat and brings back the wildest dog is elected king.

P11.2.3.p: Of two giant brothers, the one who wins the most skillful princess is elected king.

P11.3.p: Whoever owns a magic object is chosen as king.

P11.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
P11.4.p: A king is chosen on the basis of his strength and daring deeds.

P11.4.1.p: Whoever can open the palace door is made king.

P11.4.2.p: Whoever has gathered the largest fortune is made king.

P11.5.p: Whoever can fill a certain very wide seat is chosen as king.

P11.6.p: A king's inauguration is treated as his marriage to a goddess.

P12.p: Describes the character and conduct typical of kings.

P12.1.r: Penzer II 127; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
P12.1.p: A king's obsession with hunting is treated as a kind of madness.

P12.2.p: Injustice is regarded as the worst sin a monarch can commit.

P12.2.1.p: A king rules cruelly and oppressively as a tyrant.

P12.3.p: A usurper who has seized the throne imposes heavy taxes on the people.

P12.4.p: A king who plans to rape someone is killed, and his attackers flee into exile.

P12.5.p: A good king never retreats when fighting a battle.

P12.5.0.1.p: A dead king is carried into battle standing in his war-chariot, so his men believe he still fights and do not retreat.

P12.5.1.p: A king hides in a ditch during battle, with earth piled around him so he cannot be seen or retreat.

P12.6.p: A just king brings prosperity and good fortune to his people.

P12.6.1.p: A king has four duties toward his subjects: devotion to them, protecting them, judging them justly, and enlarging his kingdom.

P12.7.p: A wise king knows in advance what will happen, so nothing catches him by surprise.

P12.8.p: A king drives a nobleman out of his land in order to seize the nobleman's castle.

P12.9.p: A king shows nobility of character by resisting desire for beautiful captive women and sending them home to their people unharmed.

P12.10.p: A king is greater than everyone else in strength, beauty, size and other qualities, and usually wins contests.

P12.11.p: A king who is overly devoted to his wife neglects his royal duties.

P12.12.p: A king takes revenge on someone who fails to show him proper respect or homage.

P12.13.p: A king is quick to become angry.

P12.13.1.p: A quick-tempered king can be approached only after his anger has calmed down.

P12.14.p: A king is modest and humble rather than proud.

P13.p: Customs and traditions associated with kings.

P13.0.1.p: The special rights and privileges granted to a subordinate king or viceroy.

P13.0.2.p: The obligations owed by the attendants and followers of a subordinate king.

P13.1.p: A king is unable to pass judgment unless he is wearing his crown.

P13.2.p: Mismanaging or misusing the king's treasury is punished by death.

P13.3.p: A purple robe or golden crown is worn as the sign that someone is a king.

P13.3.1.p: Royal regalia is worn only when the king is on the battlefield.

P13.3.2.p: A ring has the power to establish or depose a king.

P13.4.p: A king is required to marry.

P13.5.p: Kings are crowned in a formal ceremony when they take the throne.

P13.5.1.p: Kings are anointed, typically with oil, as part of their crowning.

P13.6.p: By custom a man is made king for a single day and then killed at nightfall.

P13.7.p: Royal anniversaries, such as the date of a king's accession or birth, are observed with special customs or celebrations.

P13.8.p: By custom the king must not attend a funeral.

P13.9.p: Kings have special privileges or rights to certain goods or shares of produce.

P13.9.1.p: The king has the right to pick first from the spoils of war.

P13.9.2.p: The king is entitled to a fifth of everything the land produces.

P14.p: Various unusual habits or customs followed by kings.

P14.1.p: When the king wins a victory, prisoners are set free to celebrate.

P14.2.p: The king refuses to allow any one-eyed man into his presence.

P14.3.p: A king keeps playing chess even when important news is brought to him.

P14.4.p: The king demands that all the gold in the land be brought to him.

P14.5.p: The king never lets his feet touch the ground and is always carried by servants.

P14.6.p: A king or prince retreats to a special room to sulk, staying there until his wishes are granted.

P14.7.p: Entry to the king's hall is allowed only to those who have some special skill or art.

P14.8.p: The king wants no men who cannot take part in some sport or game.

P14.8.1.p: The king asks every newcomer what he can do and expects a quick answer.

P14.9.p: By law, no one may bring bad news to the king.

P14.10.p: Kings have their seat or throne located on hills.

P14.11.p: A king becomes angry at a hero who rides straight into the castle without asking permission first.

P14.12.p: A king has his own gifts stolen back from him by someone who takes them while he is not looking.

P14.13.p: A king rewards someone by giving them his own wife.

P14.14.p: A king requires everyone who comes before him to tell a story.

P14.15.p: A king keeps a champion, a strong defender, whose job is to make people respect him.

P14.15.1.p: A wise, old counsellor serves at the king's court.

P14.15.2.p: A messenger serves at the king's court to carry news and orders.

P14.16.p: A king divides his day into three parts: one for watching boys at play, one for playing the board game fidehell (possibly chess), and one for drinking.

P14.17.p: A king has his fortress or stronghold on an island.

P14.18.p: A king orders that the man whose neck the rope fits be executed, so the rope itself chooses the victim.

P14.19.p: A king goes out at night in disguise to secretly watch how his subjects live.

P14.20.p: A tom-tom drummer is sent out to announce to the people that a new king has been installed.

P14.21.p: A king appears in public only one day a year.

P14.22.p: A king keeps lions as pets and employs a lion-tamer at his palace.

P14.23.p: During years of famine a king eats very little so that he will not forget what hungry people suffer.

P15.p: A group of stories about adventures that happen to kings, often when they go among their people unrecognized.

P15.1.r: (King Alfred and the cakes.) *BP III 451 n. 1.
P15.1.p: A king in disguise is punished by a peasant, who beats him because he does not get up early enough.

P15.1.1.r: English: Wells 94 (The Taill of Rauf Coilyear).
P15.1.1.p: A peasant teaches a disguised king good manners and courtesy.

P15.1.2.p: A king pardons a person who has mistakenly called one of his courtiers king.

P15.2.p: A king demands that a subject hand over the subject's wife so the king can have her for himself.

P15.2.1.p: A king takes a subject's wife by force and keeps her as his own.

P15.3.p: A king is deprived of his realm when a pretender takes his place.

P15.4.p: A king who has criticised the work of disguised dwarf smiths is cursed by them.

P15.5.p: A king spares a man whom a rival king sent to assassinate him, because he admires the man's courage.

P15.6.p: A king goes to the bottom of the sea in a glass barrel to observe how fish live.

P15.7.p: A king works himself at a brick building so that his subjects cannot complain that he forces them to labor.

P15.8.p: Subjects drive their ruler out after he has forced them to do heavy labor.

P16.p: The ways in which a king's reign comes to an end.

P16.1.r: *Chauvin VI 194 No. 363; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
P16.1.p: A king or prince gives up worldly life and becomes a hermit or a swineherd.

P16.1.1.p: A king who retires has his own funeral rites performed for him.

P16.1.2.p: A king who learns that his queen has been unfaithful gives up his throne.

P16.1.3.p: A king gives up kingship because the higher his office, the heavier God's judgment on him; this is Cuchulinn's reason.

P16.1.4.p: A father gives up his throne in favor of his son.

P16.2.p: A king must step down if he is maimed or disfigured.

P16.2.1.p: A king must step down if he fathers an illegitimate son.

P16.3.1.1.p: Someone tries to kill an old king by smothering him in the bathroom.

P16.3.2.p: An old king too feeble to fight goes into his burial mound alive.

P16.4.r: *Wesselski Märchen 230; Icelandic: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 303, *Boberg.
P16.4.p: When a king dies, people are buried alive along with him so they can serve him in the afterlife.

P16.4.1.r: *Penzer IV 255 ff., 264; **Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 198ff., 302ff., 395ff., XV 74ff.; Chauvin VII 20; Mansikka FFC XLIII 330ff.; Hert Die Indogermanen II 440, 490ff.; Grimm Deutsche Rechtsalterthümer I 622; Hoops’ Reallexikon IV 556ff.; Schreuer Zs. f. Vgl. Rechtswissenschaft XXXIV 19ff.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Slavic: Máchal 233; India: *Thompson-Balys; Melanesia: Codrington 288ff.; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis VII 106, 227.
P16.4.1.p: A king's wife is burned alive on his funeral pyre after his death.

P16.5.p: The spear that killed a king is broken into splinters, and the shavings are thrown into a waterfall.

P16.6.p: Kings are worshipped as gods or holy beings after they die.

P16.7.p: A king is killed by members of his own household to avenge the king's deposing of his father.

P16.8.p: In a certain land every ruler dies quickly: if a king reigns one day he dies that night, and if he reigns one night he dies that day.

P16.9.p: A dead king's coffin is sunk into a river.

P17.p: Rules and stories about how the throne passes from one ruler to the next.

P17.0.1.p: A lawgiver's sons are all killed in a rebellion against him, so there is no son left to rule after him.

P17.0.2.p: A king's son becomes king when his father dies.

P17.0.2.1.p: When his son marries, the king publicly names the son as his successor.

P17.0.3.p: After someone destroys a fairy mound, vengeance from the fairies follows the king's descendants.

P17.1.r: (Cf. N683.) Hdwb. d. Märchens I 605a n. 62; India: *Thompson-Balys.
P17.1.p: The first man to arrive after a king dies becomes the heir to the throne.

P17.2.r: Serpents alleged to tell by their death which shall die first: male serpent predicts king’s death; female, queen’s. King has male serpent killed. BP IV 139; Gesta Romanorum No. 92.
P17.2.p: A queen is chosen to be spared rather than the king, so that she can bear an heir to the throne.

P17.3.p: A dying king names who will succeed him.

P17.3.1.p: The second-born son is declared successor because news of the first son's birth travelled more slowly, and the emperor will not change his proclamation.

P17.4.p: The kingship passes back and forth among brothers in turn.

P17.5.p: Brothers rule the kingdom together at the same time.

P17.6.p: The throne passes through the mother's line rather than the father's.

P17.7.p: The throne will eventually pass to the family or line that was wronged.

P17.8.r: (Cf. P17.10.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
P17.8.p: A king's kingdom passes to his younger brother instead of his older brother, who would normally inherit it.

P17.9.p: A king's illegitimate son, born outside marriage, becomes the next king.

P17.9.1.p: A king's illegitimate son is denied the throne and given only half of the inheritance.

P17.10.p: A king gives each of his three sons a kingdom, but the youngest son's kingdom is the most important one in the home country.

P17.11.p: A man who kills the king marries the king's widow and so inherits the kingdom.

P17.12.p: A king declares that whoever can carry his dead body a certain distance will succeed him as king.

P17.13.r: Answers: to study, to make pilgrimages, to build a great kingdom. Last chosen. India: Thompson-Balys.
P17.13.p: A king asks each of his three sons separately what they most desire, and the answer decides the succession.

P18.p: Stories about how kings choose or take wives and marry.

P18.1.p: After the king's much-mourned first wife dies, he marries a second wife who turns out to be an evil witch.

P18.2.p: A king who has many wives is limited in how many wives he may have.

P19.p: Other customs, powers, and events connected with kings that do not fit under the other king categories.

P19.1.p: An army can win only if the king is present with it.

P19.2.p: A king may take any woman as his lover, provided he gives her a settlement or provision.

P19.2.1.p: A king seizes a woman and takes her as his lover.

P19.3.p: A king must provide whatever visiting poets ask for, or else suffer from their satire.

P19.4.p: The special powers and privileges that belong to a king.

P19.4.0.1.p: A king's magic wand or rod, which is a symbol or source of his power.

P19.4.1.p: A king may pass judgment against everyone except one person of the highest rank in religion or learning.

P19.5.p: A king who has died is brought back to life by a saint. The note says this is an Irish myth involving the Cross.

P20.1.p: A queen who is shrewd and resourceful, often solving problems or outwitting others with her cleverness.

P21.p: A queen pleads with the king on behalf of courtiers who have been sentenced to death, saving their lives.

P21.1.r: Greek: Odyssey VI 313; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
P21.1.p: The queen acts as a go-between, speaking to the king to win mercy or favor for someone.

P22.p: A woman who was engaged to be married marries the man who murdered her fiancé, becoming queen.

P22.1.p: The queen, having married her father's and brother's killer, kills her husband to avenge them and then flees the country with her son.

P23.p: The queen urges the king to start a war for no good reason so that her sons can win land or a kingdom.

P23.1.p: The queen persuades her husband to rebel against his own overlord or superior.

P23.2.p: After her father dies, the queen persuades her husband to seize her father's kingdom for himself.

P23.3.p: The queen persuades her husband to take revenge on the killer of her father.

P23.4.p: The queen offers her own son to be killed to spur the king to fight and avenge her first husband.

P24.p: A defeated queen must pay tribute to the victorious queen in the same amount that a defeated king would have paid to a victorious king.

P25.p: A queen interferes in the affairs of government and rulership of the kingdom.

P26.r: (Cf. P16.3.0.1.) Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
P26.p: A queen who has been captured takes her own life rather than remain a prisoner.

P26.1.p: The queen kills herself after her husband defeats her father and brother in battle and has them killed.

P27.p: A king or people grieve deeply over the death of a queen.

P27.1.p: The king sits in mourning on the mound over his dead wife's grave.

P27.2.p: The king grieves so much over his wife's death that he turns to piracy, and does so again every summer afterward.

P27.3.p: The king, after remarrying, gives his daughter by the new wife the name of his first queen.

P28.p: A story element concerning the marriage of a queen, such as how she came to wed or who may win her.

P28.1.p: A female chieftain so high in rank that none of her own people dare to court or marry her.

P29.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about queens, gathering stories that concern queens in various ways.

P29.1.p: A kingdom's rule passes only to a man who is married to a particular queen; no one can become king without being her husband.

P29.2.p: A queen has an affair with her husband's foster son, the young man raised in the household.

P29.3.p: A princess who is a queen serves drink to the champions who have fought in battle.

P30.p: A general heading for motifs about princes, the sons of kings and other royal young men.

P30.1.p: The sons of a king are themselves called kings, even while young or before they rule.

P31.p: A prince is required to learn an ordinary trade or craft, despite his royal rank.

P31.1.p: Princes are trained as blacksmiths, learning to work metal.

P32.p: A prince and a commoner, a boy of ordinary birth, become friends.

P32.1.p: Every child born in the realm on the same day as the chief's son is taken to the palace to become the boy's playmates and companions.

P34.p: A prince is kept as a hostage, held captive so that the king will be kept safe from him or from rivals.

P35.p: A prince whose identity is unknown is chosen as leader of a group of children at play.

P36.r: West Africa: Frobenius Atlantis VI 182ff. No. 4.
P36.p: A prince who has lost his throne is mocked and insulted by the son of the usurper who took it.

P37.p: Birth ceremonies make an infant prince royal, so that his royal status is conferred from the start.

P38.p: A prince who fails to claim the throne loses both his father's blessing and God's blessing.

P40.p: A general heading for motifs about princesses, the daughters of kings and other royal young women.

P41.p: A princess may not marry a man of low caste, even if he passes the tests set for suitors.

P41.1.p: A great warrior is killed by the king when he asks for the princess's hand in marriage.

P50.p: A general heading for motifs about noblemen, the knights and lords who served kings.

P50.0.1.p: The duties that vassals, lesser lords sworn to serve a king, owe to their king.

P50.0.1.1.p: A king demands that the gate of a vassal's castle or city be opened to him. It shows the duty vassals owe their king.

P50.1.p: A earl, a titled nobleman ranking below a king or duke. This entry is a heading for tales about earls.

P50.1.1.p: An earl's name is held in higher esteem than the king's name, so people prefer to be known by the earl's name.

P50.2.p: A marshal, a high officer of the royal court or army. This entry is a heading for tales about marshals.

P51.p: A nobleman escapes his troubles by using his skill in a craft or trade he learned, even though he is of high birth.

P52.p: A knight takes on all challengers in a jousting tournament, fighting anyone who comes to contest him.

P52.1.p: A knight is bound to do whatever his lady commands, and must carry out her wishes as she bids.

P55.r: (Cf. F567.) Dickson 135 n. 117; Irish myth: Cross.
P55.p: A wild man, living rough in the forest, who turns out to be of noble birth.

P60.p: Noble or gentle ladies, women of high rank. This entry is a heading for tales about noblewomen.

P61.p: A noblewoman is given to foreigners on the condition that afterward their land passes through the female line, inherited by women rather than men.

P90.p: Miscellaneous tales and customs about royalty and nobility that do not fit the more specific headings.

P92.p: A bathing pool that only royalty may use; commoners are forbidden to bathe in it.

P93.p: Certain foods, ornaments, or feathers are reserved for royalty, and others may not use them.

P94.p: A person must take off their garment when in the presence of certain high chiefs.

P95.p: A nobleman in trouble asks for a favor, and it is impossible for the person addressed to refuse him.

P110.p: Royal ministers, the advisers and officials who serve a king. This entry is a heading for tales about ministers.

P111.p: A minister is banished, but the king later finds he cannot manage without him and calls him back.

P116.p: A minister serves as a stepping-stone across a trench full of fire, so the king can cross from one side to the other by stepping on him.

P120.p: Church dignitaries, such as bishops, abbots, or other high clergy. This entry is a heading for tales about them.

P150.r: Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière.
P150.p: Rich men, wealthy people of high standing. This entry is a heading for tales about the wealthy.

P151.p: A man is so wealthy that people value the dung from his mules more highly than the king's gold and silver.

P160.r: Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: Neuman.
P160.p: General motif heading for stories about beggars.

P161.p: A beggar has a great many children.

P162.p: General motif heading for stories about lepers.

P163.p: A beggar is rewarded by a king for composing a poem or song.

P170.p: General motif heading for stories about slaves.

P170.0.1.p: Female slaves are mentioned as a group.

P170.0.1.1.p: Female slaves are used as money, serving as a measure of value or means of payment.

P171.p: A person is branded, which makes him the slave of the one who branded him for the rest of his life.

P171.1.p: A slave's ear is bored as a mark of lifelong slavery.

P171.2.p: A bond woman is shown wearing a rope tied around her loins as a sign of servitude.

P172.p: A rule that slaves given as tribute must not understand the Irish language.

P173.p: The sons of a captured king are taken and made slaves.

P173.1.p: The daughter of a captured king is made a slave.

P173.2.p: A man kills an enemy's son and makes a slave of him instead, or the son is treated as a slave.

P173.3.p: Captives taken in battle are sold as slaves.

P173.4.p: An unsuccessful attempt to get rid of a man by selling him to merchants as a slave.

P174.p: The children of a free person and a slave are themselves born into slavery.

P175.1.p: A slave is hanged, usually as punishment or to end his service.

P176.p: Slaves commit murder against their masters or others.

P177.p: Explains how thralls, or unfree servants, came to exist.

P178.p: Slaves are set free, often through some unusual act or condition.

P178.1.p: Knocking out a slave's tooth gives him the right to be freed.

P178.2.p: A slave is released once a fixed term of service has run out.

P190.p: Miscellaneous motifs about social classes or ranks other than the family, such as slaves, fools and foreigners.

P191.p: The position or rights that foreigners have in society.

P192.p: Madmen and professional fools, who are often treated as special figures in society.

P192.1.p: A person who works as a professional fool, entertaining or serving others by acting foolishly.

P192.2.p: A fool who turns out to be a shrewd judge and settles cases wisely.

P192.3.p: A fool who is able to walk on water.

P192.4.p: A fool who is able to live under water.

P192.5.p: A fool who befriends birds and wild animals.

P192.6.p: A custom in which the heads of madmen are shaved so that others can recognize them as demented.

P192.7.p: A fool who can be identified by a lump on his forehead.

P200.p: Miscellaneous motifs about family life and relationships between relatives.

P201.p: Hostility that exists between members of the same family as a standing condition.

P201.1.p: A feud between two branches of the same family.

P202.r: Irish myth: Cross; Koryak: *Jochelson JE VI 372.
P202.p: A person is criticized or mocked for having no relatives.

P203.r: N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 225.
P203.p: A boy interrupts a game played with the bones of his father or another relative who was murdered, bringing the crime to light.

P205.p: A person refuses to fight against their own relatives, even when pressed to do so.

P210.p: A general motif about the relationship between a husband and a wife.

P211.r: S. A. Indian (Carib): Alexander Lat. Am. 266.
P211.p: A wife must choose between supporting her husband and supporting her father in a feud between them.

P211.1.r: (Cf. P253.3.) Only one can be saved; he alone is irreplaceable. Spanish: Childers.
P211.1.p: A wife chooses her father over her husband or her son.

P211.2.p: A mother kills her husband because he murdered their daughter.

P212.p: A wife shows more mercy than her blood relatives: when they refuse to pay ransom to free a condemned man, she pays it herself.

P213.p: A husband shows more mercy than his blood relatives: when they refuse to pay ransom to free a condemned woman, he pays it himself.

P214.p: A wife drinks the blood of her slain husband.

P214.1.p: A wife dies by suicide or otherwise dies when her husband dies, after drinking his blood.

P216.p: A wife is the only person who is able to persuade her husband to do something.

P230.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 527a s.v. “Eltern und Kinder”; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
P230.p: A general motif about the relationship between parents and their children.

P230.1.p: A mother favors her son and a father favors his daughter.

P230.2.p: A mother dislikes her children because they were born of a marriage she was forced into.

P230.3.p: A queen dislikes her son because he is unlike her and loves a poor girl, so she plots against him.

P231.p: A general motif about the relationship between a mother and her son.

P231.1.p: A boy becomes sick with grief after his mother dies.

P231.2.p: A son warns his mother of danger.

P231.3.p: A mother's love for her child, shown as a motif of devotion.

P231.4.p: A mother kills her sons because they lack the courage to help her avenge her father and brothers, and are likely to betray her plot.

P231.5.p: A mother reveals that her son's father is a supernatural being.

P231.6.p: A mother eagle drives out a dull, stupid changeling child and raises a bold, energetic son instead.

P231.7.p: A mother kills herself when her son wants to marry a foreigner and follow the foreign wedding customs.

P232.p: A general heading for stories about the relationship between a mother and her daughter.

P232.1.p: A wicked mother and her sons do everything they can to stop her daughter from marrying the man she loves.

P232.2.p: A mother arranges for her daughter to unknowingly marry her own father, as revenge for his raping her.

P233.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
P233.p: A general heading for stories about the relationship between a father and his son.

P233.1.p: A son is handed over as a pledge or hostage in place of his father, who has committed a murder.

P233.2.p: A young hero is scolded or rebuked by his father.

P233.2.1.p: A father drives away a bad son whom the mother favors.

P233.3.p: Berserk warriors scold their father for calling their enemy invincible, though he seemed to have no reason to say so.

P233.3.1.p: A hero's son by a giantess scorns his father as feeble, but it is the son who is killed.

P361.7.p: A captain refuses to reveal his king's secret, even though he is pressed to do so; he will not betray where recruits are being raised.

P361.8.p: A faithful servant endures torture rather than betray or abandon his master.

P361.9.p: A crow lets itself be caught in order to save the king of the crows.

P362.p: A faithful servant is put in charge of raising and educating the crown prince.

P365.p: A servant who is disloyal and betrays his master.

P365.1.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 209; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
P365.1.p: Disloyal menservants corrupt the maids in the household.

P365.2.p: A servant plans to take his master's possessions, having already taken his master's wife.

P366.p: A master orders his servant to tell him both his faults and his good qualities, frankly and without flattery.

P400.r: **Sébillot Légendes et Curiosités des Métiers (Paris, n.d.); Jewish: Neuman.
P400.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about different trades and professions people work at.

P401.p: A son insists on learning his father's trade, even though the dying father had kept it secret because it had not brought him success. The son finds out the secret from his mother.

P410.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about laborers, people who do hard manual work for a living.

P411.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about peasants, poor country people who farm the land.

P411.1.r: (Miller of Sanssouci.) Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 309 No. 13.
P411.1.p: A peasant turns down the king's offer to buy his possessions and keeps what he has.

P411.1.1.p: A peasant and his wife live in a simple hut near the castle, in contrast to the king and queen living in luxury.

P411.2.p: A peasant is chopping wood in front of his house when guests arrive.

P411.3.p: A wounded hero seeks shelter in a peasant's house and is healed there.

P411.4.p: A hero accidentally arrives at a peasant's house, spends the night there, and receives advice and directions.

P412.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about shepherds, people who tend flocks of sheep or other animals.

P412.1.p: A shepherd is the main hero of the story.

P412.1.1.p: A shepherd's simple life is considered the right training for someone who will later become a ruler.

P412.2.p: A swineherd, a person who tends pigs, appears as a character.

P412.3.p: The hero works as a herder of rabbits.

P413.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about ferrymen, people who carry passengers across a river or water.

P413.1.p: A ferryman who never stops carrying passengers and who takes the ruler's place when the ruler is in danger.

P413.1.1.p: The ferryman hands an oar to the king, and the king is then bound to remain a ferryman.

P414.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about hunters, people who hunt wild animals for food or sport.

P415.p: A general heading for stories and motifs about colliers, people who make or sell charcoal.

P415.1.p: A hero is a collier, a person who works as a charcoal burner or coal miner.

P420.p: A general heading for stories about learned professions, such as judges, lawyers, physicians, scribes, and clergy.

P421.p: A judge appears in the story as a character.

P421.1.p: Jackals act as judges, deciding cases or passing judgment.

P422.p: A lawyer appears in the story as a character.

P422.1.p: Lawyers are punished in hell after death.

P422.1.1.r: Scala Celi 7b No. 44; Etienne de Bourbon No. 440.
P422.1.1.p: When a dead lawyer's tongue is examined, it is found to be lacking, meaning it has no good words or honesty in it, so he is condemned.

P424.r: Penzer X 263a s.v. “Physician”; Irish myth: Cross.
P424.p: A physician, or doctor, appears in the story as a character.

P424.1.r: He does not want to see those who have died from his medicine. *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 259 No. 204.
P424.1.p: A physician hides his eyes as he passes a graveyard.

P424.2.p: A doctor who can cure illness can also poison people, and this realization makes the king suspicious of him.

P424.3.p: A physician is killed because he predicted a patient's death.

P424.3.1.p: A physician who is called skillful is forced to help carry away the bier of his dead patient.

P424.4.p: A fairy works as a physician, healing people.

P425.p: A scribe, or professional writer, appears in the story as a character.

P425.1.p: A scribe is unable to read his own handwriting.

P426.p: A member of the clergy, such as a priest or cleric, appears in the story as a character.

P426.0.1.p: Pagans, fearing the clergy, flee into fairy mounds (hills).

P426.1.p: A parson, or priest, appears in the story as a character.

P426.1.1.p: The first of the animals and fruits belongs to the priest, as his due.

P426.2.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 507b; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Espinosa II No. 75, Espinosa Jr. No. 186.
P426.2.p: A hermit, a person who lives alone apart from society, usually for religious reasons.

P426.3.p: Monks, members of a religious community who live under vows in a monastery.

P426.3.1.p: An untrained monk suddenly becomes a skilled craftsman, such as a smith or wright, through the power of a saint.

P426.3.2.p: Monks are presented as druids who have been converted to Christianity, taking over the role of the old pagan priests.

P426.3.3.p: A woman disguises herself as a monk and gets into a monastery.

P427.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 311.
P427.p: A druid, a learned man or poet in old Celtic society who was also a priest, judge, or keeper of lore.

P427.0.1.p: A druid is so respected and feared that people stand in awe of him.

P427.0.2.p: A person who is attacked or cursed by a druid loses a treasure.

P427.0.4.p: Simon Magus, the magician of the New Testament, is cast as a druid.

P427.1.p: A druid performs sacrifices as part of his religious duties.

P427.1.2.p: Druids serve as priests, leading the religious worship of their people.

P427.1.3.p: A baptism performed by druids in the old pagan religion.

P427.1.4.p: A special haircut or shaved head marking a druid.

P427.2.p: A druid goes as a messenger seeking peace between opposing sides.

P427.3.p: A druid gives advice or instruction to someone.

P427.4.p: A druid poet uses satire, mocking verse, to attack people.

P427.4.1.p: The fear of a druid's satirical mockery is what makes something happen or what forces a person to act.

P427.5.p: A druid works as a physician, healing the sick.

P427.5.1.p: Wounded soldiers are healed by bathing in a pool of milk, through the magic power of a druid.

P427.6.p: A druid serves as a judge who settles disputes.

P427.7.p: A poet, a learned man of the kind who composes verse and holds traditional knowledge.

P427.7.1.p: A poet who makes up a poem or song on the spot, without preparation.

P427.7.2.p: A poet who knows a very large number of poems, stories, or verses by heart.

P427.7.2.1.p: Poets use language that is difficult or obscure, so ordinary people cannot understand them.

P427.7.2.1.1.p: Poets and fools are regarded as closely related, since both are thought to speak in odd or foolish ways.

P427.7.4.p: A poet who is a woman.

P427.7.5.p: A bard, a poet-singer who recites or sings heroic and historical verse.

P427.7.6.p: A poet carries a rod of office, a sign of the poet's authority or rank.

P427.7.7.p: A poet who serves as a judge who decides cases.

P427.7.8.p: A poet is rewarded with a gift or payment for composing a poem.

P427.7.9.p: Poets are driven out or exiled from a place.

P427.7.9.1.p: Poets make such excessive demands for payment or hospitality that people become angry and drive them away.

P427.7.10.p: Poets compete against one another, trying to outdo or outshine each other.

P427.8.p: Druids build raths, the earthen ringforts of Ireland.

P427.9.p: Druids, acting as poets, boil a spell or magic potion in a cauldron.

P428.p: A musician, a person who makes a living by playing music.

P428.1.p: A harper, a musician who plays the harp.

P429.p: A general heading for learned professions that do not fit a more specific category, such as scholarly or scientific callings.

P429.1.p: Tales or sayings in which astronomers, people who study the stars, appear as a type.

P430.p: A general heading for folk characters who are moneylenders, financiers, or merchants.

P431.p: A general heading for merchant characters, traders who buy and sell goods for profit.

P431.1.p: Merchants carry news from place to place, so they become the means by which stories and information spread.

P435.p: A general heading for usurers, people who lend money at high interest.

P435.1.p: A wealthy moneylender prays that the sons of rich people will go mad, which would help his lending business; his own sons then lose their minds.

P435.2.p: A usurer stops lending money, not out of principle but because lending is costing him money.

P440.p: A general heading for craftsmen and skilled workers who make or repair things by hand.

P441.r: *Fb “skrædder”; *Chauvin IX 29 No. 18; *Sébillot Métiers No. 7; *Feilberg Dania I 165ff., III 184ff.; Paludan Danske Studier (1925) 19ff.; Missouri French: Carrière.
P441.p: A general heading for tailor characters, who sew and make clothing.

P441.1.p: A tailor sits on God's throne for a single day.

P441.2.p: Tailoring is the one trade the devil cannot learn, because he cannot tie a knot in thread without making the sign of the cross.

P441.3.p: A tailor is punished in hell after death.

P441.4.p: A busy tailor asks a soldier to stand guard in his place, and the soldier ends up doing the tailor's duty.

P442.p: A general heading for baker characters, people who bake bread for a living.

P442.1.p: A baker and the devil walk together, usually as companions on a journey.

P443.r: Type 461 (Danish); Von Sydow Våra folksagor (1941) 38; *Sébillot Métiers No. 1; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 137, 141, 198.
P443.p: A general heading for miller characters, people who run a mill for grinding grain.

P443.0.1.p: A miller whose mill is powered by water flowing from a stream or millrace.

P443.1.p: An explanation for why millers are considered thieves, often because they keep part of the grain as payment.

P444.p: A general heading for cabinet-makers, craftsmen who build fine furniture.

P444.1.p: A brave soldier and a timid cabinet-maker travel together as companions, and the story turns on the contrast between their characters.

P445.p: A general heading for stories about weavers, a trade of people who make cloth on a loom.

P445.1.p: Explains why weavers are the most unhappy of men, because a weaver once gave a nail used in the Crucifixion of Jesus.

P445.2.p: Explains why weavers are known for patience, usually as a tale origin for that trait.

P446.r: Sébillot Métiers No. 11; Penzer III 100 n. 1.
P446.p: A general heading for stories about barbers, the men who cut hair and shave beards.

P446.1.p: Barbers who ruin or bungle carefully made plans, so the scheme fails because of them.

P446.2.p: Barbers portrayed as sly and greedy, looking to cheat or profit at others' expense.

P447.r: *Sébillot Métiers Nos. 17, 18; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 257—67; Andree (1878) 153; *Nyrop Dania IX 186ff.; Von Sydow Våra folksagor (1941) 39ff. — Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman.
P447.p: A general heading for stories about smiths, craftsmen who work metal in a forge.

P447.0.1.p: A smith who comes from Lochlann, a name for Scandinavia that here may also refer to an otherworld, with the exact origin uncertain.

P447.1.p: A smith who turns out to be the grandfather of a king.

P447.2.p: A smith who builds a rath, an ancient earthen fort or ring-shaped enclosure.

P447.3.p: A smith who is lord of a hall where hospitality is offered to guests.

P447.4.p: A smith who is punished in hell for his misdeeds.

P447.5.p: A king honors a smith because the king cannot do without him.

P447.6.p: Two or more smiths compete with one another, each trying to outdo the other.

P447.7.p: A goldsmith who becomes a lover, usually pursuing or winning a woman.

P447.8.p: A goldsmith who is greedy and covets wealth, often at others' expense.

P448.p: A general heading for stories about butchers, the men who slaughter and cut up animals for meat.

P451.p: A general heading for stories about spinners, people who twist fibre into thread.

P452.r: Type 326; German Grimm No. 4; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 269f.; Sébillot Métiers No. 8.
P452.p: A general heading for stories about dressmakers and milliners, people who make or trim clothing and hats.

P453.r: **C. Nyrop Dania VIII 195ff.; *Sébillot Métiers No. 10; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 151, 155—157, 185.
P453.p: A general motif about shoemakers as a trade in folk narrative.

P453.1.p: Shoemakers are lazy and sluggish because of a curse: a shoemaker spat at Christ on the way to the crucifixion, and Christ declared that he and all shoemakers after him would be poor and slobbering.

P454.p: A general motif about hatters, people who make or sell hats, as a trade in folk narrative.

P455.p: A general motif about masons, or bricklayers, as a trade in folk narrative.

P456.r: Sébillot Métiers No. 13; Panchatantra (tr. Ryder) 62ff., 89ff., 260ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
P456.p: A general motif about carpenters as a trade in folk narrative.

P457.p: A general motif about house painters as a trade in folk narrative.

P458.r: Types 327, 700; Köhler Aufsätze 49; Sébillot Métiers No. 16; Missouri French: Carrière.
P458.p: A general motif about woodsmen, people who cut and work with wood or forests, as a trade in folk narrative.

P459.p: A general heading for other craft workers not listed separately under artisans.

P459.1.p: A printer appears as a character in the tale.

P460.p: A general heading for other trades and professions not listed elsewhere.

P461.r: *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 485ff.; Missouri French: Carrière.
P461.p: A general motif about soldiers as characters in folk narrative.

P461.1.p: A soldier whose hands have both been cut off keeps fighting with his teeth until he is killed.

P461.2.p: A soldier dies happily after learning that the enemy has been routed or defeated.

P461.3.p: A soldier ordered to set fire to an enemy fleet is caught and sawed in two.

P461.4.p: A woman teaches the art of fighting with weapons to a soldier or others.

P471.p: A general motif about actors as characters in folk narrative.

P471.1.p: Actors are banished from a place together with vagabonds and beggars.

P475.r: Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman.
P475.p: A general motif about robbers as characters in folk narrative.

P475.1.p: A band of twelve robbers appears in the tale.

P481.r: Penzer X 77a s.v. “Astrologer”; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
P481.p: An astrologer: a person who reads the stars to predict the future or advise others.

P482.p: A painter, a person who makes pictures as an artist.

P482.1.p: The devil snatches a painter up out of his chair.

P483.p: A juggler or conjurer who performs tricks and sleight of hand for an audience.

P485.p: A philosopher, a thinker who studies wisdom and the nature of things, appearing as a character type in folk narrative.

P485.1.p: Philosophers who are treacherous or deceitful toward others.

P500.p: Government: the rule of a country or the authority that governs people.

P510.r: *E. v. Künssberg Rechtliche Volkskunde (Halle, 1936); **Spargo Juridicial Folklore in England (Durham N.C., 1944); Irish myth: Cross.
P510.p: Law courts: the places and proceedings where judges try cases and pass sentence.

P511.p: A condemned criminal is allowed to choose how he will be executed.

P511.1.r: (Cf. J1181.) Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Friedrich der Grosse” n. 58.
P511.1.p: The condemned criminal chooses to die of old age instead of by violent execution.

P511.2.r: Herbert III 71; Hervieux IV 310 No. 117; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
P511.2.p: A man sentenced to lose an eye is allowed to pick the tool used to take it.

P512.r: *Fb “gifte” I 432; Zs. f. Vksk. XXIII 108, XXV 286, XXVII 236; Sehreuer Zs. f. vgl. Rechtswiss. XXXIV 201; Blätter f. pommersche Volkskunde VII 63.
P512.p: A condemned woman can be saved from execution if a rogue agrees to marry her.

P512.1.p: A condemned man is released from execution at a woman's request, on condition that he marries her.

P513.p: A criminal may choose to fight against overwhelming odds instead of being put to death by the court.

P515.p: A criminal is pardoned, but the pardon arrives after he has already been executed.

P516.p: The youngest judge is the first to give his decision.

P517.p: A crime is treated as less serious because it was committed at a lady's request.

P518.p: Cities set up as places of refuge where people accused of crimes or fleeing vengeance can find safety.

P521.p: A judge who is too pleased with himself ignores a criminal's confession. After torturing the man without result, the judge releases him, and the man says he was about to confess everything; the judge lets him go anyway.

P522.p: Laws: the rules a community or state sets and enforces.

P522.1.r: (Cf. P535.) Irish myth: Cross (P548.2); India: Thompson-Balys; New Guinea: Ker 61.
P522.1.p: The law of retaliation: one life must be paid for each life taken, so feuding sides must each give up equal numbers.

P522.1.1.p: Retaliation in kind: a person who has lost a nose is awarded the loss of another's nose as legal compensation. It is an example of the 'eye for an eye' principle of law.

P523.p: Rules about who is allowed to bring a lawsuit or case before a court.

P523.1.p: A foreigner is not permitted to bring a lawsuit in court.

P523.2.p: A madman is not permitted to bring a lawsuit in court.

P523.2.1.p: A fool cannot be punished for his crime, because he is not legally responsible for what he does.

P523.3.p: A slave is not permitted to bring a lawsuit in court.

P524.p: Rules about legal security, where one person guarantees another's obligation or appearance in court.

P524.1.p: A poet is not allowed to serve as legal security or guarantor for someone else's obligation.

P524.2.p: A foreigner is not allowed to serve as legal security or guarantor for someone else's obligation.

P525.p: Rules and cases concerning contracts and agreements.

P525.0.1.p: A legal saying holding that a promise made creates a debt that must be paid.

P525.1.p: A contract made by a madman is not valid and cannot be enforced.

P525.2.p: A contract made by a woman without her husband's consent is not valid.

P525.3.p: The closest blood relative of a murdered man must take revenge for his death.

P526.p: General legal principles or maxims applied in judging cases.

P526.1.p: A legal principle that the calf belongs to the cow is applied to decide who owns a copy of a manuscript, so the copy goes to the owner of the original.

P526.2.p: A legal principle that the son belongs to his mother: when a child's legitimacy is doubted, the child is not held guilty.

P531.p: Taxes, fines, and tribute paid to a ruler or to a conquering power.

P531.1.p: A tribe that fails to attend its yearly feast must send a gift as a sign that it submits to the ruler.

P531.1.1.p: Conquered foreigners are required to pay tribute to their conquerors.

P531.2.p: A tax is levied on treasure that is found hidden or buried, so the finder must hand part of it to the authorities.

P532.p: A ruler or people is required to pay tribute, a regular payment of goods or money, to a more powerful overlord.

P533.p: A feudal arrangement in which lord and vassal regularly exchange specified services, aid, and gifts.

P533.1.p: A person is given up as a hostage to guarantee that a feudal tribute or agreement will be kept.

P533.1.1.p: Boys, rather than adults, are handed over as hostages to secure a feudal agreement.

P535.p: A fixed money payment, called an eric fine, is imposed as compensation for injuring someone or other wrongs, instead of other punishment.

P536.p: A person is punished for not paying a tax or tribute owed to the authorities.

P536.1.p: A person's nose is cut off as punishment for failing to pay a tax.

P537.p: A regular payment of wages or a salary is made to a person for their service.

P541.p: A community or ruler makes laws, the making of laws as a motif.

P541.1.p: Laws are made in groups of seven at a time.

P541.2.p: Laws are made at a yearly feast or festival gathering.

P541.2.1.p: Laws are made at a feast held only once every seven years.

P548.p: Various other customs connected with legal proceedings and courts that do not fit a more specific heading.

P550.r: *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 181—254; Jewish: Neuman.
P550.p: Matters concerning warfare, soldiers, and the military as a part of government.

P551.p: A general motif about armies, the organized bodies of soldiers a ruler raises for war.

P551.0.1.p: An army made up of a band of full-time, professional fighters.

P551.1.p: An army consisting of young men.

P551.2.p: Soldiers are chained or tied together so that none can flee from the battle.

P551.3.p: Members of the clergy are excused from serving in the army.

P551.4.p: A hero single-handedly drives back warriors who are fleeing the battlefield and forces them to fight again.

P551.5.p: A corps or unit made up of boys serving as soldiers.

P551.6.p: A law requiring women to do military service is cancelled because a saint intervenes on their behalf.

P551.7.p: A person gets into trouble or quarrels with the officials who are recruiting soldiers.

P551.8.p: Vassal warriors owe no obligation to fight for their overlord unless they are paid.

P551.8.1.p: Only 700 subjects of a lesser king must answer the call to serve a higher overlord in any one levy.

P551.9.p: Semen that is believed to make men warlike, a 'battle seed' passed on to produce fierce fighters.

P552.p: Ways of arranging troops for battle, meaning the formations an army takes up on the field.

P552.1.p: Warriors fight standing in a circle around their leader, forming a defensive ring.

P552.2.p: The best soldiers are spread out among the rest of the army so that their fighting skill does not stand out.

P552.3.p: A tight military formation of soldiers standing close together in rows with overlapping shields and spears.

P552.3.1.p: Soldiers hold their shields overhead, overlapping like a roof, to protect themselves from missiles.

P552.4.p: Siege engines or other mechanical weapons used in war.

P552.5.p: A warrior gets a haircut in preparation for going to war.

P553.p: Weapons used in fighting, such as swords, spears, and arrows.

P553.1.p: Weapons smeared or treated with poison so that any wound they cause is deadly.

P554.p: After a battle, the dead are counted by a pile of stones: each survivor takes one stone away, and the number left shows how many died.

P555.p: A side is beaten in battle.

P555.1.p: A defeated warrior shows surrender by lying down with the victor's sword held between his teeth.

P555.2.p: The bodies of slain enemies are cut into pieces.

P555.2.1.p: After a battle, the severed heads of the defeated enemies are heaped together as a trophy.

P555.2.1.1.p: The heads of slain enemies are put on public display as proof of victory.

P555.2.1.2.p: A slain opponent's jawbone is cut off and taken as a trophy.

P555.3.p: When a town or castle is captured, its gate is enlarged so that the conqueror's spear can be carried through it crosswise, a sign of total subjection.

P556.p: A warrior issues a formal invitation to fight a battle or duel.

P556.1.p: The challenger signals a challenge by turning the left side of his shield toward the enemy.

P556.2.p: A challenge to battle is made by throwing a javelin up into the sky.

P557.p: Various accepted rules and practices followed in warfare.

P557.1.p: A warrior captured without his weapons cannot demand ransom for his release.

P557.2.p: A pledge or promise made to an enemy must be honored.

P557.3.p: Stones are raised on the spot where an enemy falls in battle, as a memorial.

P557.4.p: Accepted rules govern one-on-one combat between two warriors.

P557.4.1.p: The first warrior to reach the field of combat gets to choose the weapons.

P557.4.2.p: A warrior who has started a combat may stop it if he wishes.

P557.4.3.p: In a multi-day combat, the choice of weapons changes each day in turn.

P557.4.4.p: A challenger to single combat must accept the same conditions that he imposed on the person he challenged.

P557.4.4.1.p: When a two-armed warrior fights a one-armed opponent, he binds one of his own hands to his side to make the contest even.

P557.5.p: A warrior who kills people under his protection is disgraced.

P557.6.p: A warrior dies facing the enemy, never turning his back.

P557.7.p: Men divorce their wives before going off to war.

P561.r: **R. C. Clephan The Tournament (London, 1919); *O. Mueller Turnier und Kampf in den altfrz. Artusromanen (Erfurt, 1907); Jewish: Neuman.
P561.p: A general heading for stories about tournaments, the medieval contests in which knights fought for prize and honor.

P561.1.p: A king who has banned tournaments is talked into lifting the ban.

P561.2.p: A tournament is held in order to take revenge for the death of a king.

P600.p: A heading for Jewish customs, as recorded in the Neuman material, that are described as strange or unusual.

P611.r: Icelandic: Snorra Edda Skaldsk. XLI (Nibel), *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
P611.p: Women meet and talk while bathing together.

P612.p: A trumpet is blown in front of the house of a person who has been condemned to death.

P613.p: A coin is placed in the dead person's mouth to pay Charon, the ferryman who carries souls across the river Styx to the underworld.

P616.p: Newcomers are forced to spend the night with the ruling princess. They are given a sleeping potion, and if they fail to consummate the marriage, their goods are confiscated.

P617.p: People weep when a child is born, and at burials they sing and laugh instead.

P621.p: When a horse is bought, the bridle is handed over with it as part of the sale.

P622.p: A servant must keep the horns and hide of cattle that have been slaughtered.

P623.p: A general heading for fasting used as a way to force someone to pay or comply, called distraint, where a person fasts to put pressure on another.

P623.0.1.p: A person fasts in order to pressure God.

P623.0.1.1.p: Clerics fast against God in order to obtain a revelation from him.

P623.0.2.p: A person fasts in order to pressure the Devil.

P623.0.3.p: A person fasts in order to pressure fairies.

P623.0.4.p: A person fasts in order to pressure saints.

P623.0.5.p: Saints fast so that a tree worshipped by pagans falls down.

P623.0.6.p: A saint fasts to force people to pay the saint's dues.

P623.0.7.p: Calves are kept away from cows during a fast, as a way of putting pressure on people.

P631.p: A visiting nobleman is given precedence, so he passes first through a narrow path ahead of the host. The motif sets this as a custom.

P632.p: Customs by which people's social rank is shown and recognized, such as through seating, food, or dress.

P632.1.p: Men of high rank are given couches to recline on, marking their status.

P632.2.p: Cuts of meat are handed out according to each person's rank.

P632.2.1.p: The choicest portion of meat at a feast is reserved for the bravest warrior.

P632.3.p: Children's rank is recognized by the quality of their furnishings and food.

P632.4.p: The color a person wears shows their rank.

P632.4.1.p: Rank is shown by the position or color of a shield or flag.

P632.5.p: Heroes of Irish legend value long hair as a mark of honor.

P633.p: Custom that young people may not go ahead of their elders.

P634.p: Customs and practices connected with holding feasts.

P634.0.1.p: Customs connected with eating and food in general.

P634.1.p: A feast of hospitality lasts for three days and three nights.

P634.2.p: A feast of hospitality lasts for seven days and seven nights.

P641.p: A wronged husband will not kill a man who is naked, since it would shame him to do so.

P642.p: Custom that only brave men may wear beards.

P643.p: A hero goes to a fight unarmed except for weapons he has taken from his opponent.

P644.p: A hero refuses to answer questions until he has been dressed.

P651.p: Customs involving the hanging or use of bells.

P651.1.p: Bells are hung at every corner of a ship.

P651.2.p: Bells are fastened to a horse's mane.

P651.3.p: Bells are rung in reverse order as a way of raising an alarm or signaling danger.

P661.p: A sick person is kept in a separate hut or shelter so that the bad smell from their illness does not spread to others.

P665.p: A custom in which a man boasts openly about his sexual prowess.

P671.p: A woman covers her face with a veil to show that she is astonished or amazed.

P672.r: E. Hinojosa Homenaje a Menéndez y Pelayo I 568ff.; R. Menéndez Pidal Cantar del Mio Cid II 498; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
P672.p: Grabbing or pulling a man's beard is treated as an insult.

P672.1.p: A fur robe is made from the beards of defeated kings.

P672.2.p: Cutting off a man's or woman's hair is done as an insult.

P672.3.p: The shaved head of a hero is rubbed with cow dung as an insult.

P672.4.p: A king's moustache is used to light a lamp, as an insult to the king.

P673.p: Washing another person's feet is a sign that a quarrel has been made up.

P674.p: An old person kills himself when he is no longer strong enough to live usefully.

P675.p: Touching the head is the sign that a bargain has been accepted.

P676.r: Greek: Iliad XXII 337 and passim; India: Thompson-Balys.
P676.p: A supplicant grabs another person's feet or legs to beg for mercy or a favor.

P677.p: Customs connected with duels between men.

P677.1.p: In a duel, the two fighters take turns shooting arrows and catching them.

P678.p: Pulling out one's own hair is a sign of grief.

P678.1.p: Tearing one's clothes is a sign of grief.

P681.p: General customs connected with mourning for the dead.

P682.1.p: A greeting is made by invoking God's name.

P682.2.p: Sailors have the right to put the first question to a landsman (someone who is not a seaman) they meet, under a Jewish greeting custom. The motif concerns the custom itself rather than a plot.

P710.p: A general heading for motifs about nations as whole peoples or countries.

P711.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
P711.p: Love of one's country and loyalty to one's nation, shown as a virtue in stories.

P711.1.p: A man values the wolves of his own country more than the dogs of another country, showing preference for what is native.

P711.2.p: The mother of a soldier who has been crippled in war tells him that every limp step will remind him of his courage.

P711.3.r: Gives his own funds. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
P711.3.p: An ordinary citizen saves his country's honor through a brave or loyal act.

P711.4.p: Scipio leaps into a burning pit to save Rome from destruction, sacrificing himself for his city.

P711.5.p: A Roman takes on the task of killing Hannibal but kills another man by mistake; as punishment for his failure he burns off his own hand.

P711.6.p: A nation keeps its unity by driving out all foreign people living among it.

P711.7.p: Aristotle gets out of his sickbed and hurries into battle to fight for his country.

P711.8.p: A person has a strong dislike of being buried in foreign ground, away from their homeland.

P711.9.p: A king learns that the nation whose king dies in battle will win, and so he lets himself be killed to secure victory for his people.

P715.p: A heading for motifs about particular named nations or races of people.

P715.1.p: Motifs concerning Jews as a particular people.

P720.p: A heading for motifs about the size and growth of populations.

P721.p: Diseases such as plague are called upon to reduce a population that has grown too large.
